newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia stocks mostly lower, Manila, Jakarta hard-hit.
newsitem.headline: Asia stocks mostly lower, Manila, Jakarta hard-hit.

text.p: Most Asia stock markets ended lower on Tuesday, with shares in the Philippines and Indonesia particularly hard hit by heavy selling by local investors and foreign funds.
Thai shares, which continued to erode throughout most of the session, staged a dramatic late recovery after local mutual funds followed a government request to boost the market.
Even Hong Kong shares fell slightly in a modest adjustment after Monday's nearly 228-point advance.
Hong Kong had been one of the few markets to follow the record gains made in New York on Friday after news of weaker-than-expected U.S. employment figures.
Philippine stocks posted the largest decline in terms of a percentage on Tuesday with the main index falling 83.49 points, or 2.68 percent, to 3,037.54.
"We have a very depressed market today and it's because of mixed local and foreign selling," said Teresa Lee, a trader at Lippo Securities.
Indonesian shares were not far behind, falling 11.531 points, or 1.97 percent, to 574.78.

The market was hurt by heavy selling in cigarette company PT Hanjaya Mandala Sampoerna and other selected blue-chip stocks, such as PT Telekomunikasi Indonesia, the country's leading provider of telecommunications services.

Thai stocks, which dropped more than six percent on Monday to the lowest level in more than three years, fell around 2.00 percent on Tuesday before recovering ahead of the close on local mutual fund buying, brokers said.
The key index ended up 11.71 points, or 1.24 percent, at 956.34. Despite the improvement, the closing level was still the lowest since the August 25, 1993 closing of 952.33.
The country's finance minister, Bodi Chunnananda, said he would ask local private and public rescue funds to help shore up the battered stock market.

A senior official at Thailand's Finance Ministry told reporters the market was likely to remain volatile until a new government is formed after general elections on November 17. Some dealers in the Philippines and Thailand attributed the declines to selling by various foreign funds that were pulling money out of those markets to invest in Hong Kong.
But many Hong Kong fund managers disagreed.
One regional strategist said funds have been flowing into Hong Kong for a long time.

"Funds flowing into Hong Kong -- that's been the case for some time now," said David Semple, regional strategist at Peregrine Investment. "This is not something that suddenly happened yesterday," he said.
"We've been aggressively overweight Hong Kong for some time now," said Robert Rountree, regional strategist at Nomura Research Institute (Hong Kong) Ltd.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng index erased earlier gains and shed 26.31 points, or 0.22 percent, to end at 12,106.76.

"The market has run up something like 1,000 points in the last few weeks and although we remain positive for the long term...the market probably looks a little bit overbought at these levels," said Keith Irving, head of research at HG Asia.

Elsewhere, Malaysian stocks succumbed to some profit-taking and were off 5.42 points, or 0.47 percent, at 1,143.08, while Singapore's Straits Times Index was down 10.62 points, or 0.50 percent, at 2,116.04.
Taiwan shares also lost ground, shedding 35.51 points, or 0.54 percent, to 6,584.91 in a correction to its recent rise.
Australia's All Ordinaries Index ended down 8.1 points, or 0.35 percent, at 2,331.7, while New Zealand share were down 9.38 points, or 0.41 percent at 2,265.38.
Korean shares proved the exception and closed 2.29 points, or 0.29 percent, higher at 797.62.
At 1109 GMT, the dollar was at 111.08/1.13 yen and 1.5250/57 marks.
SIMEX North Sea Brent crude oil futures fell in late trading to $24.40 a barrel, down nine cents from London's settlement.
